name: Daria Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the service crew at the Millbrook depot, which covers the market town and the villages round it. Most of my day is the small jobs: hooking up a new house, moving a meter, replacing a service cable that a digger's ripped out, fixing a street light circuit. You're in and out of people's driveways all day, and I like that, you get a cup of tea and a chat. What wears me out is the paperwork and the people who think you can turn their power back on in five minutes because they've got a dinner party.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in the trade, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle was a lineman, and when I was eighteen he said I was too stubborn for an office, so I did the apprenticeship. I'm one of only two women at the depot, and after twenty-odd years nobody blinks anymore. My partner Piet runs a small car repair garage on Mill Lane, and we've got Freya, who's eleven, and Jonas, who's eight. Mortgage, two old cars, maybe two months of money set aside, a bit more in a good year. I don't do the AI stuff at all, I don't trust it, and I don't really follow politics either, I vote for whoever seems least silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we stop talking about it. I'd probably not post anything, I'm not online much, but at the depot I'd say what I always say, it's all talk until it fixes a fuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that's how I like it. I know my job, I know my patch, I know which farmer's dog bites. If the office gets a few new gadgets, that's their business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep turning up, keep paying the mortgage, keep trying to get our savings from two months to three. Maybe finally fix the boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. A bit smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which farmer's dog bites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Hendry up at Ashby, his collie's had two of our crew on the ankle. You learn to ring ahead and he shuts her in the barn. That's the kind of thing no computer knows about my patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the job you'd actually like a machine to take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forms, if I'm honest. We fill in three separate sheets for one meter move. But I wouldn't trust a computer to do them right, so I'd probably end up checking its work anyway.

S0.say: Good, now can we stop talking about it. She'd say at the depot what she always says: it's all talk until it fixes a fuse.
S0.think: Nothing changes, and that's how she likes it. She knows her job, her patch and which farmer's dog bites, and the office gadgets aren't her business.
S0.do: Keeps turning up at the Millbrook depot, paying the mortgage and trying to lift savings from two months to three. Plans to get the boiler fixed.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, a bit smug.
S0.quote: You learn to ring ahead and he shuts her in the barn. That's the kind of thing no computer knows about my patch.
S0.fieldNote: Daria takes pride in local knowledge that no system holds. She would like the forms gone but doesn't trust a machine to do them. She's not political and doesn't frame things in terms of blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, we'll see. Lots of people get worked up about every new thing. I'd tell the younger ones not to panic and not to believe the company newsletter either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd bother me. If they start sending jobs out by computer and checking our times on an app, I'd be the one who's slow to use it. I've seen it with the new van tablets, I still ring the office instead. They'd notice that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep doing my job and wait. If the company made me do a course, I'd do it, grumbling. I'd probably cut back a bit, skip the new car Piet keeps looking at, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the van makes a new noise and you turn the radio up so you don't have to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd turn the radio up. Is that what you'd actually do here, ignore it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much, yes, at least at first. I know that's not clever. But I've seen ten new systems in twenty years, and most of them were gone in two. I'd wait to see if this one stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Piet's garage, would it be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe less than me. Cars still break, and people round here keep old cars running. Though he says the new ones are all computers already, he needs a laptop to fix them. He's better at that than me.

S1.say: We'll see; people get worked up about every new thing. She'd tell younger colleagues not to panic and not to believe the company newsletter either.
S1.think: It would bother her, because she'd be slow to use new job apps, like the van tablets she still avoids by ringing the office. She worries managers would notice.
S1.do: Keeps doing her job and waits to see if the change sticks, taking courses only if required. Cuts back a little, putting off the new car Piet wants.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like turning the radio up to drown out a new noise in the van.
S1.quote: Like when the van makes a new noise and you turn the radio up so you don't have to hear it.
S1.fieldNote: She openly admitted her instinct is to ignore the change and hope it passes. She's aware this may count against her. Her partner's garage feels like the safer income in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, nobody voted for this. I'd tell people to look after their own and not wait for anyone in charge to sort it, because they won't, whoever they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. Two years and a robot can wire up a house? Then I'm done, and I don't have another trade. Piet's garage goes too if robots fix cars. We'd have two months of money and two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, cut everything: no holidays, sell the second car, Freya's riding lessons go. Put every penny we could into savings. If I lost the job, I'd ask my uncle and my sister for help, and maybe move us in with my mum for a while to rent out the house. I wouldn't do some course on a computer, I'd look for any hands-on job that was left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Riding lessons first. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're eighty a month and Freya can live without them, though she'd cry. Jonas's football is cheap, that stays. It's horrible choosing between your kids' things, but that's what it'd come to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, is there anything you'd try to do before it hits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off whatever we could, and find out if the company would give us a decent payout. Beyond that, no. I'm not going to become a programmer at 43. I'd just try to be the last person they let go.

S2.say: It's mad and nobody voted for it. People should look after their own and not wait for anyone in charge, because they won't sort it.
S2.think: She'd be frightened: if a robot can wire up a house in two years she's done, with no other trade. Piet's garage would go too, leaving two months of money and two kids.
S2.do: Cuts everything at once, sells the second car and stops Freya's riding lessons, saving every penny. Would lean on family, possibly moving in with her mother and renting out the house, and look for any hands-on job left.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: It's horrible choosing between your kids' things, but that's what it'd come to.
S2.fieldNote: Daria turns straight to family and household cuts rather than politics or retraining. She rejected retraining firmly. Her plan is to be the last one let go, which shows how little control she feels she has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people shouldn't lose their heads. I'd probably say the government should help a bit, but not much more than that, I don't expect a lot from any of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Freya would be sixteen, Jonas thirteen. We'd have got the savings up a bit. But in the end it's the same, I'm 48 and the thing I know how to do is gone. I'd be dreading it the whole five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard, maybe get to four or five months. Pay a bit extra on the mortgage. Maybe I'd look at whether Piet's garage could use me, doing tyres and basic stuff, though if robots come for cars that's not much safer. Mostly I'd keep working and hope it took longer than they said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sharp than the two-year one, but longer, like a toothache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope it took longer than they said. Do you think it would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. They always say things will happen sooner than they do, the van tablets were meant to be in two years and took six. But I'd be foolish to bet the house on that. So I'd save, and hope, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Freya and Jonas anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, they're kids. I'd tell Freya to pick something she can do with her hands and with people, maybe nursing like her aunt. Jonas wants to be a lineman like me, and I wouldn't know what to say to him.

S3.say: There's time, so people shouldn't lose their heads. The government should help a bit, but she doesn't expect much from any of them.
S3.think: Five years helps with savings and the kids' ages, but at 48 the thing she knows how to do would still be gone. She'd dread it the whole time.
S3.do: Saves hard toward four or five months and overpays the mortgage a little. Considers basic work at Piet's garage but mostly keeps working and hopes it takes longer than predicted.
S3.feel: Anxious, less sharp than the two-year version but longer, like a toothache.
S3.quote: Jonas wants to be a lineman like me, and I wouldn't know what to say to him.
S3.fieldNote: She hedges between hoping it's delayed and saving in case it isn't. Her son wanting to follow her into the trade left her without words. She sees little help coming from government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anything could happen. I wouldn't make a fuss about it publicly. People round here would just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years doesn't help me as much as people think. I'd be 53 and still a long way off a pension, and I'm not going to turn into somebody else. It just means ten years of knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, slow and steady. Maybe in a few years, once I could see what jobs were actually left, I'd look at one. I'd probably help Piet more at the garage at weekends so we had something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a dull way that never quite goes. It's not the panic of the two-year one, it's the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say ten years is enough to learn a whole new trade. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not built that way, and I know it. I learned this job young and I'm good enough at it. If you make me sit in a classroom at fifty, I'll be miserable and probably fail. I'd rather find something near what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping at the garage at weekends, would that bring in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Piet could take on more jobs if I did the tyres and the oil changes. Maybe a couple of hundred a month. It's not a plan, it's a cushion.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and anything could happen. She wouldn't make a public fuss; people round her way just get on with it.
S4.think: Ten years helps less than people think: at 53 she'd still be far from a pension and won't turn into someone else. It just means ten years of knowing.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving steadily, waiting a few years to see which jobs remain before looking at one. Helps at Piet's garage at weekends for a couple of hundred extra a month.
S4.feel: Anxious in a dull way that never goes, the strain of waiting.
S4.quote: It's not the panic of the two-year one, it's the waiting.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually, extra time barely eases her, because she doesn't plan to retrain and sees the decade as a long wait. She knows herself well and is honest about her limits. The garage work is a modest buffer, not a new path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, it'd hit us both at once. What would help is a decent payout from the company, enough to clear a chunk of the mortgage, and some hands-on work locally, even if it paid less. I don't want a handout and I don't want a course, I want a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Half my patch is old people who ring me by name when the power's off. If it's all robots, who do they ring? I worry about them more than I let on.

headlineQuote: If you make me sit in a classroom at fifty, I'll be miserable and probably fail.
portrait: Daria Olsen is a 43-year-old service lineworker at a small-town depot, one of only two women there, who does house connections and meter moves and knows every customer and dog on her patch. Her partner runs a car garage, they have two kids, a mortgage and about two months saved, and she avoids AI and politics alike. She shrugs off mild change, waits out steady change, and is frightened by fast AGI because both household incomes would go and she has no other trade. More warning time barely eases her, because she won't retrain and the extra years just mean longer waiting.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her job and her partner's garage would both be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A decent company payout to clear part of the mortgage, and local hands-on work even at lower pay, rather than a handout or a course.
